content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.75. The test results were very noisy (the same task gave 49, 48, 1 and 8), so this rests on averages over repeated tests rather than any single clear result. I used 51 of the 60 budget.

The design was to pick a test task built entirely from known rules but looking unlike any trained task (L1-S1-M2, similarity 0.375). I compared it against tasks with new rules that look similar overall to what was trained, then kept retesting it as its rules appeared in more trained tasks.

| Stage | Trained so far | Task tested | Mean examples needed (runs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | each rule once (2 tasks) | L1-S1-M2: no new rules, similarity 0.375 | 33 (8) |
| 1 | | L4-S4-M4: 3 new rules, similarity 0.56 | 20, median 8 (7) |
| 1 | | L1-S1-M4: 1 new rule, similarity 0.75 | 25 (5) |
| 2 | L1, S1, M2 each in 2 tasks | L1-S1-M2 | 31.5 (6) |
| 3 | L1, S1, M2 each in 3 tasks | L1-S1-M2 | 28.7 (12) |
| 3 | | L1-S1-M4 | 18 (6) |

The tasks added in stages 2 and 3 were chosen so that L1-S1-M2 never became more similar to anything trained. That way any drop in its cost would come from its rules becoming reusable parts, not from similarity.

- **Against part-based:** in stage 1, the task with no new rules was no cheaper than tasks with new rules. The one with three new rules was actually cheaper.
- **Against factor-when-justified:** L1-S1-M2 stayed roughly flat after its rules appeared twice (rules out k=2) and three times (rules out k=3). In stage 3, the similar-looking L1-S1-M4 was still cheaper, even though it has a new rule and L1-S1-M2 doesn't.

The main weakness is that the change from 33 to 28.7 for L1-S1-M2 is small next to the noise. A modest factoring effect at k=3 can't be fully excluded, which is why the confidence is 0.75 rather than higher.
